rows.stem: Which of the following curve represents the first order reaction ?

options.label: A
options.text: A plot of \(t_{1/2}\) (vertical axis) against \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) (horizontal axis) : a straight line of positive slope rising from the origin.

options.label: B
options.text: A plot of \(t_{1/2}\) (vertical axis) against \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) (horizontal axis) : a horizontal straight line.

options.label: C
options.text: A plot of Rate (vertical axis) against Concentration (horizontal axis) : a horizontal straight line.

options.label: D
options.text: A plot of Rate (vertical axis) against Concentration (horizontal axis) : a curve falling steeply and then levelling off.

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — The FOUR OPTIONS ARE THEMSELVES GRAPHS — there is no option text on the page at all, only four labelled plots with printed axis labels (t½ vs [R]0 for A and B, Rate vs Concentration for C and D). The axis labels above are read verbatim off the page; the CURVE SHAPES are described in words because an MCQ needs four distinguishable option texts and a duplicate pair would otherwise be produced. The real crops should be attached. Page idx 4.
rows.solution: For a first order reaction the half-life is \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\), and that expression contains no concentration term at all. So however much reactant you start with, the time taken for half of it to disappear is the same, and a plot of \(t_{1/2}\) against \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) is a horizontal straight line. A line rising from the origin would mean \(t_{1/2}\) is proportional to \([\mathrm{R}]_0\), which is zero order behaviour, since there \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{2k}\). The two Rate-against-Concentration plots describe something else again: a horizontal one is zero order, while first order gives a straight line through the origin rather than a curve that levels off.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Which of the following solutions will have the lowest freezing point in water ?
rows.solution: Depression of freezing point is a colligative property, \(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m\), so the solution with the most dissolved particles freezes lowest. All four are \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\), which leaves the van't Hoff factor to decide. Glucose and urea are non-electrolytes and do not dissociate, so \(i = 1\) for both. Potassium chloride gives two ions per formula unit, so \(i = 2\). Calcium chloride gives one \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) and two \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\), so \(i = 3\) and it produces three times as many particles as the glucose solution. The \(0.1\ \mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{CaCl_2}\) solution therefore has the lowest freezing point.

rows.stem: Which of the following is \(\underline{\text{not}}\) a transition metal ?
rows.solution: A transition metal is one with a partially filled d subshell either in its ground state or in one of its common oxidation states. Scandium is \(3d^1 4s^2\); copper reaches \(3d^9\) as \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\); silver reaches \(4d^9\) as \(\mathrm{Ag^{2+}}\). All three qualify. Mercury is \([\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{14}5d^{10}6s^2\), and its common ion \(\mathrm{Hg^{2+}}\) is \(5d^{10}\), so the d subshell is completely filled throughout and mercury is not a transition metal. Zinc and cadmium are left out of the series for exactly the same reason.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Which of the following represents the fraction of molecules with energies equal to or greater than \(\mathrm{E_a}\) ?
rows.solution: In the Arrhenius equation \(k = A e^{-E_a/RT}\) the exponential term is not merely algebra: it is the fraction of molecules whose energy equals or exceeds the activation energy. So the quantity asked for is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\). The two bare ratios \(+\dfrac{E_a}{RT}\) and \(-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}\) are exponents rather than fractions and are not confined between 0 and 1, and \(e^{+E_a/RT}\) is greater than 1 for every positive activation energy, which no fraction can be.

rows.stem: What will happen during the electrolysis of aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{CuCl_2}\) by using platinum electrodes ?

options.label: B
options.text: \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas will be released at cathode

options.label: C
options.text: \(\mathrm{O_2}\) gas will be released at anode

options.label: D
options.text: \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas will be released at anode

rows.solution: Two reductions compete at the cathode: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\), with \(E^{\circ} = +0.34\) V, and the reduction of water to hydrogen. Copper has the higher reduction potential, so copper metal is deposited and no hydrogen is released; and deposition is a cathode process in any case, never an anode one. At the anode the competition is between oxidising water to \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and oxidising \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) to \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\). On standard potentials alone water should win, but oxygen evolution on platinum carries a large overpotential, so in practice chlorine is what appears: \(2\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2} + 2e^-\). Chlorine gas is released at the anode.

rows.stem: Aspirin is obtained by acetylation of
rows.solution: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, made by acetylating the phenolic \(-\mathrm{OH}\) of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride. Salicylic acid is 2-hydroxybenzoic acid, which carries both the ring \(-\mathrm{OH}\) that gets acetylated and the \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) that survives into the product. Phenol and benzoic acid each have only one of those two groups, and salicylaldehyde has a \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) where aspirin needs a \(-\mathrm{COOH}\).

rows.stem: The secondary valency of Co in the complex \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\) is
rows.solution: In Werner's theory the primary valency is the oxidation state and is satisfied by negative ions, while the secondary valency is the coordination number, the count of ligand donor atoms bonded directly to the metal. Inside the coordination sphere of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]^{2+}}\) there are five ammonia molecules and one nitrito group, each donating a single pair of electrons, so six donor atoms surround the cobalt and the secondary valency is 6. The primary valency here is 3, which is the oxidation state of the cobalt.

rows.stem: At low temperature, phenol reacts with dil. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) to yield
rows.solution: The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group activates the ring strongly and directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions, so phenol is nitrated by dilute nitric acid at low temperature, conditions far milder than benzene needs. Under those mild conditions only one nitro group enters, and it enters at both available sites, so the product is a mixture of ortho-nitrophenol and para-nitrophenol, separable afterwards by steam distillation. Concentrated nitric acid is what gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, and since both isomers form, neither of the two answers containing the word only can hold.

rows.stem: Which of the following is ‘not’ true about enantiomers ?

options.label: A
options.text: They have the same chemical reactivity.

options.label: B
options.text: They have the same specific rotation.

options.label: C
options.text: They have the same melting or boiling point.

options.label: D
options.text: They have the same refractive index.

rows.solution: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, so every property measured in an achiral environment is identical for the pair: melting point, boiling point, refractive index, density, solubility and chemical reactivity towards achiral reagents. What separates them is their behaviour towards plane-polarised light. Their specific rotations are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, one dextrorotatory and the other laevorotatory, so the claim that enantiomers have the same specific rotation is the statement that is not true.

rows.stem: Aniline on direct nitration yields
rows.solution: Nitration is carried out in a strongly acidic mixture, and in that medium most of the aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion. The \(-\mathrm{NH_3^+}\) group is deactivating and meta directing, while the small amount of free aniline still present is activated and ortho, para directing. The two pathways run side by side, so the product is a mixture in which the para and meta isomers dominate: 51% para, 47% meta and only 2% ortho, the ortho position being further suppressed by the bulk of the substituent.

rows.stem: Which of the following amines has lowest \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) value ?
rows.solution: A lower \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a stronger base. All four have nitrogen attached to a benzene ring, so in each the lone pair is partly delocalised into the ring and less available for a proton; what separates them is how far that is offset. Every methyl group on nitrogen pushes electron density towards it by the inductive effect, so basicity rises in the order aniline, then N-methylaniline, then N,N-dimethylaniline. The para-nitro compound is weakest of all, since the nitro group withdraws electrons both inductively and by resonance. The strongest base, and so the one with the lowest \(\mathrm{pK_b}\), is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-N(CH_3)_2}\).

rows.stem: The deficiency of which of the following vitamins causes increased fragility of red blood cells and muscular weakness :
rows.solution: Vitamin E is the fat-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes, including those of red blood cells, against oxidative damage. Take it away and the membranes are left unprotected, which is why its deficiency shows up as increased fragility of red blood cells together with muscular weakness. Deficiency of vitamin A causes xerophthalmia and night blindness, of vitamin K poor clotting of blood, and of vitamin D rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : It is not possible to separate the components of an azeotrope by fractional distillation.
Reason (R) : Components of an azeotrope have the same composition in liquid and vapour phase and boil at a constant temperature.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: An azeotrope boils at a constant temperature and gives off vapour of exactly the same composition as the boiling liquid. Fractional distillation works only because ordinary vapour is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it came from, so that repeated vaporisation and condensation gradually separates the two. When the vapour and the liquid have identical compositions there is nothing left for successive vaporisations to enrich, and the mixture distils over unchanged. Both statements are true, and the second states exactly why the first holds, so the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The presence of –OH group in phenols directs the incoming group to meta position in the ring.
Reason (R) : –OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution reaction.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group donates its lone pair into the ring by resonance, and that builds up negative charge at the positions ortho and para to it. This is what makes phenol far more reactive than benzene towards electrophiles, so the Reason is a true statement. But the same resonance also fixes where the electrophile attacks: it goes to the ortho and para positions, which are the electron-rich ones, and not to meta. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
Reason (R) : Actinoids are radioactive in nature.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Actinoids do show a wide range of oxidation states, and they are radioactive, so both statements are true on their own. The two facts have unrelated causes, though. The wide range of oxidation states comes from the very small energy gap between the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals, which lets comparable numbers of electrons be lost from all three. Radioactivity is a property of the nucleus, arising from nuclear instability, and has nothing to do with valence electrons. So both statements are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The pentaacetate of glucose does not react with \(\mathrm{H_2N-OH}\).
Reason (R) : It indicates the presence of free – CHO group in glucose.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Glucose pentaacetate has all five of its hydroxyl groups acetylated, and it does not react with hydroxylamine, so the Assertion is a true statement. The inference drawn from it is the wrong way round. Hydroxylamine reacts with a free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group to give an oxime, so a failure to react is evidence that no free \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group is present, not that one is. This observation is one of the pieces of evidence for the cyclic hemiacetal structure of glucose. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
What type of deviation from Raoult’s law is shown by a mixture of phenol and aniline ? Give reason.
What will happen to the boiling point of the solution on mixing phenol and aniline ?
rows.solution:
A mixture of phenol and aniline shows negative deviation from Raoult's law. Hydrogen bonding between the phenolic proton and the lone pair on the nitrogen of aniline is stronger than the hydrogen bonding that exists in pure phenol or in pure aniline, so after mixing the molecules are held in the liquid more tightly than they were before. Fewer of them escape into the vapour, each partial vapour pressure falls below the value Raoult's law predicts, and the total vapour pressure of the mixture is lower than expected.

Because the vapour pressure has been lowered, the mixture must be heated to a higher temperature before its vapour pressure can match the external pressure. The boiling point of the solution therefore increases.

rows.stem: Why are haloarenes less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ? Give two reasons.
rows.solution:
Any two reasons are enough here.

Resonance: the lone pair on the halogen is delocalised into the ring, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond takes on partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger than the pure single bond in a haloalkane, and correspondingly harder for a nucleophile to break.

Hybridisation: the carbon carrying the halogen is \(sp^2\) in a haloarene against \(sp^3\) in a haloalkane. An \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character and is the more electronegative, so it holds the shared pair of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond more tightly.

Two further reasons would serve equally well: the electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud of the ring repels the approaching nucleophile, and the phenyl cation that a unimolecular route would have to pass through is highly unstable.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination compounds :
(i) \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2][Ag(CN)_2]}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
rows.solution:
(i) The compound is built from a complex cation and a complex anion, and the cation is named first. In \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}\) the two neutral ammine ligands leave silver at \(+1\). In \(\mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^-}\) two cyanido ligands carry \(-2\) against an overall \(-1\), so silver is \(+1\) again, and an anionic complex takes the Latin stem of the metal with the ending -ate. The name is diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I).

(ii) Oxalate is a bidentate ligand carrying \(-2\), so three of them contribute \(-6\); the three potassium ions contribute \(+3\), which leaves iron at \(+3\). The complex ion is the anion, so iron takes its Latin stem with the -ate ending, and the name is potassium trioxalatoferrate(III).

rows.stem:
(i) Give a chemical test to show that \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\) are ionisation isomers.
(ii) What is meant by the ‘Chelate effect’ ? Give an example.
rows.solution:
(i) The two compounds put a different ion inside the coordination sphere, so each leaves a different ion free in solution, and a test for the free ion tells them apart. Adding silver nitrate solution to \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) gives a white precipitate of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\), because its chloride is the counter ion and is free; \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\) gives no precipitate, since its chloride is bound to the cobalt. The test also works the other way round: barium chloride solution precipitates white \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) from \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\), whose sulphate is free, but not from \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\).

(ii) The chelate effect is the extra stability a complex gains when a bidentate or polydentate ligand binds the same metal ion through two or more donor atoms and so closes a ring. For example \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\), in which each of three ethane-1,2-diamine molecules forms a five-membered ring with the cobalt, is far more stable than \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) with its six separate ammonia ligands.

rows.stem:
Differentiate between the following :
(i) Peptide linkage and Glycosidic linkage
(ii) Essential amino acids and Non-essential amino acids
rows.solution:
(i) A peptide linkage is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CONH}-\) formed when the \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group of one amino acid condenses with the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group of the next and a molecule of water is lost; it is what joins amino acid residues into a protein. A glycosidic linkage is the oxygen bridge formed when two monosaccharide units join through their hydroxyl groups, again with loss of water; it is what joins sugar units into di- and polysaccharides.

(ii) Essential amino acids are those the body cannot synthesise for itself and must obtain ready-made from the diet. Non-essential amino acids are those the body can synthesise on its own.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Following reaction takes place in one step :
\(\mathrm{2A + B \longrightarrow 2C}\)
How will the rate of above reaction change if the volume of the reaction vessel is decreased to one third of its original volume ? Will there be any change in the order of reaction with the reduced volume ?
rows.solution:
The reaction is stated to take place in one step, so it is elementary and its rate law can be read straight off the balanced equation, with the stoichiometric coefficients as the exponents:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}]\)

Compressing the vessel to one third of its volume does not change how much A or B is present, but it confines the same amount to a third of the space, so each concentration is tripled. The new rate is
\(k[3\mathrm{A}]^2[3\mathrm{B}] = 27\,k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}]\)
so the rate increases 27 times.

The order is a feature of the rate law itself, not of the concentrations at which it is evaluated, so it does not change: it remains \(2 + 1 = 3\).

rows.stem:
For the first order thermal decomposition reaction, following data was obtained :
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_4(g) + HCl(g)}\)

| S. No. | Time(s) | Total Pressure (atm) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0.30 |
| 2 | 30 | 0.50 |

Calculate rate constant.
[Given : log 3 = 0.48]
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the working is correct throughout, but the final answer is printed as \(0.037\ \mathrm{atm^{-1}}\). A first order rate constant has units of reciprocal time, because the logarithm it multiplies is a pure number, so the answer is \(0.037\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). Pressure appears in this calculation only as a way of measuring concentration, and it cancels inside the logarithm.]

Let \(P_i\) be the initial pressure of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\) and let \(x\) be the pressure of it that has decomposed by time \(t\). Each molecule that decomposes produces one \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) and one \(\mathrm{HCl}\), so the total pressure at time \(t\) is
\(P_t = (P_i - x) + x + x = P_i + x\)
which gives \(x = P_t - P_i\). The pressure of undecomposed \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\) remaining is therefore
\(P_i - x = 2P_i - P_t\)

For a first order reaction,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{P_i}{2P_i - P_t}\)

Putting in \(P_i = 0.30\) atm and \(P_t = 0.50\) atm at \(t = 30\) s,
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{30}\log\dfrac{0.30}{2(0.30) - 0.50} = \dfrac{2.303}{30}\log\dfrac{0.30}{0.10} = \dfrac{2.303}{30}\log 3\)
\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{30}\times 0.48 = 0.037\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

rows.stem:
Answer the following :
(i) Why is the Equilibrium Constant \(\mathrm{(K_c)}\) related to \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{cell}}\) and not to \(\mathrm{E_{cell}}\) ?
(ii) Two metals ‘A’ and ‘B’ have standard electrode potential values of \(-0.24\) V and \(+0.80\) V respectively. Which of these will liberate hydrogen gas from dil. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) ?
(iii) Write the cell reaction which occurs in lead storage battery when it is in charging.
rows.solution:
(i) At equilibrium the cell reaction has no net tendency to go either way, so the cell delivers no potential and \(E_{cell} = 0\). Putting that into the Nernst equation gives
\(0 = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c\)
so \(K_c\) is fixed by \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\) alone. This has to be so: \(E_{cell}\) depends on whatever concentrations happen to be in the cell at that moment and drifts as the reaction proceeds, whereas an equilibrium constant is a fixed number for a given reaction at a given temperature. Only \(E^{\circ}_{cell}\), which is also fixed, can determine it.

(ii) Metal 'A' will liberate hydrogen. A metal displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid only if it is a stronger reducing agent than hydrogen, which means its standard electrode potential must be negative. The value for 'A' is \(-0.24\) V, so it is oxidised in preference to hydrogen and reacts with dilute \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to give the gas. The value for the other metal is \(+0.80\) V, which is positive, so it lies below hydrogen in reducing power and cannot displace it.

(iii) Charging drives the discharge reaction backwards, rebuilding the two electrodes and regenerating the acid:
\(2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{Pb(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)}\)

rows.stem: What type of battery is Mercury cell ? Why it is more advantageous than dry cell ? Write overall reaction taking place in Mercury cell.
rows.solution:
A mercury cell is a primary cell: its reaction cannot be reversed by passing current back through it, so once the reactants are used up the cell is finished and cannot be recharged.

Its advantage over the dry cell is that it holds a constant potential difference, about \(1.35\) V, throughout its working life. The dry cell's voltage falls steadily as it is used, because the ammonium chloride paste is consumed and the concentrations of the ions in its electrolyte keep changing. In the mercury cell the overall reaction involves only solid and liquid species, with no ion whose concentration appears in the Nernst expression, so nothing shifts the potential as the cell runs down. That steadiness is why it suits hearing aids and watches.

The overall reaction is
\(\mathrm{Zn(Hg)} + \mathrm{HgO(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{ZnO(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)}\)

rows.stem: Calculate the boiling point of a solution containing 0.61 g of benzoic acid (Molar mass = 122 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) in 5 g of \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) in which it dimerises to the extent of 88%. The boiling point and \(\mathrm{K_b}\) of \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) are 46.2 °C and 2.3 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) respectively.
rows.solution:
Benzoic acid associates into dimers in carbon disulphide, so the solution contains fewer particles than the formula mass would suggest and the van't Hoff factor is less than 1. For association of \(n\) molecules into one,
\(\alpha = \dfrac{1-i}{1 - \dfrac{1}{n}}\)
and with \(n = 2\) and \(\alpha = 0.88\),
\(0.88 = \dfrac{1-i}{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}} = 2(1-i)\)
so \(i = 1 - 0.44 = 0.56\).

The molality of the solution is
\(m = \dfrac{0.61/122}{5/1000} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.005} = 1.0\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Therefore
\(\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m = 0.56 \times 2.3 \times 1.0 = 1.288\ \mathrm{K}\)

and the boiling point of the solution is
\(T_b = 46.2 + 1.288 = 47.488\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), that is \(320.638\ \mathrm{K}\).

rows.stem:
Write the reactions of D-Glucose with the following :
(a) HI
(b) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water
(c) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Heated with hydriodic acid over a long period, glucose is reduced right down: every oxygen is stripped away and the six-carbon chain survives intact as \(n\)-hexane.
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_4CH_3}\)
This is the reaction that established that glucose has an unbranched chain of six carbon atoms.

(b) Bromine water is a mild oxidising agent and attacks only the aldehyde group, leaving the primary alcohol untouched. The product is the monocarboxylic gluconic acid.
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
That this reaction fails with fructose is how the aldose is distinguished from the ketose.

(c) Concentrated nitric acid is the stronger oxidising agent and oxidises both ends of the chain, the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) and the primary \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\), to \(-\mathrm{COOH}\). The product is the dicarboxylic saccharic acid.
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling point than alcohols of comparable molecular masses.
(b) Alpha \((\alpha)\) hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature.
(c) Nucleophilic addition of ammonia and its derivatives does not occur with carbonyl group in strongly acidic medium.
rows.solution:
(a) Carboxylic acid molecules associate in pairs through intermolecular hydrogen bonds, each molecule donating its \(-\mathrm{OH}\) proton to the carbonyl oxygen of the other, so in the liquid they exist largely as cyclic dimers. Two hydrogen bonds have to be broken for each pair to separate, which takes more energy than breaking the single hydrogen bond linking one alcohol molecule to the next. The boiling point is correspondingly higher.

(b) The \(\alpha\) hydrogen sits on the carbon next to the carbonyl group, which withdraws electrons strongly. When that proton is removed the resulting carbanion is not left to carry its charge alone: the charge is delocalised onto the electronegative carbonyl oxygen. It is this resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base that makes the \(\alpha\) hydrogen acidic.

(c) Ammonia and its derivatives attack the carbonyl carbon using the lone pair on nitrogen. In a strongly acidic medium that lone pair is taken up by a proton, so the reagent is converted into its conjugate acid and stops being a nucleophile altogether. The reaction therefore needs a weakly acidic medium, around \(\mathrm{pH}\ 4.5\): acidic enough to protonate the carbonyl oxygen and activate it, but not so acidic as to destroy the nucleophile.

rows.stem:
Write the reaction involved in the following :
(a) Reimer-Tiemann reaction
(b) Kolbe’s reaction
(c) Friedal-Crafts acylation of anisole
rows.solution:
(a) Reimer-Tiemann reaction. Phenol treated with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide generates dichlorocarbene, which attacks the ring at the position ortho to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\); acidification of the intermediate then gives salicylaldehyde.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) } \mathrm{H^+}]{\text{(i) } \mathrm{CHCl_3} + \text{ aq. } \mathrm{NaOH}} \text{2-hydroxybenzaldehyde}\)

(b) Kolbe's reaction. Phenol is first converted with aqueous sodium hydroxide into sodium phenoxide, which is a stronger nucleophile than phenol itself. Carbon dioxide then attacks the ring ortho to the oxygen, and acidification gives salicylic acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. } \mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{CO_2}} \text{2-hydroxybenzoic acid}\)

(c) Friedel-Crafts acylation of anisole. Anisole with acetyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride gives the ortho and para acetyl derivatives, since \(-\mathrm{OCH_3}\) is activating and ortho, para directing; the para compound, 4-methoxyacetophenone, is the major product.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. } \mathrm{AlCl_3}} \text{2-methoxyacetophenone} + \text{4-methoxyacetophenone}\)

rows.stem:
Compound ‘X’ with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) reacts with aqueous KOH to give an alcohol. The rate of this reaction depends only on the concentration of the compound ‘X’. When an optically active isomer ‘Y’ of the compound ‘X’ was treated with aqueous KOH solution, the rate of reaction was found to be dependent on concentration of compound ‘Y’ and aqueous KOH both.
(a) Write down the structural formula of both ‘X’ and ‘Y’.
(b) Out of ‘X’ and ‘Y’, which one will undergo racemisation and why ?
(c) Out of ‘X’ and ‘Y’, which one will form product with inversion of configuration and why ?
rows.solution:
(a) The rate for 'X' depends only on the concentration of 'X', so 'X' reacts by the unimolecular route, \(\mathrm{S_N}1\), and the isomer of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) that ionises most readily is the tertiary one:
\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-Br}\), 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
The rate for 'Y' depends on the concentrations of both the halide and the hydroxide, so 'Y' reacts by the bimolecular route, \(\mathrm{S_N}2\); 'Y' is also optically active, which requires a carbon bearing four different groups, and that points to the secondary halide:
\(\mathrm{Y} = \mathrm{CH_3-CHBr-CH_2-CH_3}\), 2-bromobutane.

(b) 'X' is the one that undergoes racemisation. Its \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) route passes through a planar carbocation intermediate, which the nucleophile can attack with equal ease from either face, so both configurations are formed in equal amounts. Strictly, racemisation can only be observed in a product from a starting material that was itself optically active, and 'X' is not chiral; the marking scheme accordingly awards full marks to a student who answers 'Y' here instead.

(c) 'Y' is the one that gives a product with inverted configuration. In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the nucleophile attacks from the side directly opposite the leaving group, and as the new bond forms and the old one breaks in the same step the other three bonds are pushed through to the far side, inverting the configuration at that carbon.

rows.stem:
(i) Why \(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2}\) is a stronger base than \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) in aqueous solution ?
(ii) Write structural formulae of the compound A and B :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOBr}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow[\text{Base}]{\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl}} \mathrm{B}\)
rows.context: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salts shows that these are basic in nature. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia whereas aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia. Aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution reaction. The main problem encountered during electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic amines is that of their high reactivity. Substitution tends to occur at ortho-and para-positions. Hinsberg reagent is used for the identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Aryldiazonium salts, usually obtained from arylamines, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
(i) Three effects decide basicity in aqueous solution, and they do not all point the same way. The inductive effect of the methyl groups pushes electron density onto nitrogen and favours \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\). Against that, three bulky methyl groups crowd the nitrogen and hinder a proton from reaching the lone pair. More important still is solvation: the cation \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3NH^+}\) has only one hydrogen on nitrogen available for hydrogen bonding to water, whereas \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_3^+}\) has three, so the conjugate acid of the primary amine is far better stabilised by the solvent. In water the steric and solvation factors outweigh the inductive one, so \(\mathrm{CH_3-NH_2}\) is the stronger base.

(ii) Sodium hypobromite brings about the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which converts an amide into a primary amine with one carbon fewer, so
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\)
Benzoyl chloride in the presence of a base then benzoylates that amine at nitrogen, so
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3-NHCOC_6H_5}\)

rows.stem: A compound ‘X’ with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_9N}\) reacts with Hinsberg reagent to give a product insoluble in alkali. Identify ‘X’.
rows.context: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salts shows that these are basic in nature. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia whereas aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia. Aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution reaction. The main problem encountered during electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic amines is that of their high reactivity. Substitution tends to occur at ortho-and para-positions. Hinsberg reagent is used for the identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Aryldiazonium salts, usually obtained from arylamines, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulphonyl chloride. With a primary amine it gives a sulphonamide that still carries a hydrogen on nitrogen; that hydrogen is acidic, so the product dissolves in alkali. With a secondary amine the nitrogen has no hydrogen left after the reaction, so the sulphonamide has nothing acidic and is insoluble in alkali. A tertiary amine does not react at all.

A product insoluble in alkali therefore identifies a secondary amine, and the only secondary amine with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_9N}\) is N-methylethanamine, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH-CH_3}\).

rows.stem: How can you convert aniline to benzonitrile ?
rows.context: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salts shows that these are basic in nature. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia whereas aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia. Aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution reaction. The main problem encountered during electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic amines is that of their high reactivity. Substitution tends to occur at ortho-and para-positions. Hinsberg reagent is used for the identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Aryldiazonium salts, usually obtained from arylamines, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
Diazotise the aniline, then replace the diazonium group by cyanide. Aniline treated with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid at \(273-278\ \mathrm{K}\) gives benzenediazonium chloride, and warming that with cuprous cyanide, the Sandmeyer reaction, gives benzonitrile.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273-278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2} + \mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCN}} \mathrm{C_6H_5CN}\)

rows.stem: Why is \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group of aniline acetylated before carrying out nitration ?
rows.context: The reaction of amines with mineral acids to form ammonium salts shows that these are basic in nature. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia whereas aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia. Aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides, anhydrides and esters by nucleophilic substitution reaction. The main problem encountered during electrophilic substitution reactions of aromatic amines is that of their high reactivity. Substitution tends to occur at ortho-and para-positions. Hinsberg reagent is used for the identification and distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Aryldiazonium salts, usually obtained from arylamines, undergo replacement of the diazonium group with a variety of nucleophiles to provide advantageous methods for producing aryl halides, cyanides, phenols and arenes.
rows.solution:
The \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group activates the ring so powerfully that direct nitration is difficult to control and gives a mixture of products. There is a second and worse problem: the nitrating mixture is strongly acidic, and in it aniline is largely protonated to the anilinium ion, whose \(-\mathrm{NH_3^+}\) group is meta directing, so a substantial meta product appears alongside the ortho and para ones.

Acetylating the nitrogen first converts \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) into \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\). This group is still ortho, para directing but much less strongly activating, and it is not protonated under the reaction conditions. Nitration then proceeds under control and gives the para derivative as the major product, after which the acetyl group is removed by hydrolysis to recover the amine.

rows.stem: In octahedral crystal field, energies of which d-orbitals will be raised when ligands approach the central metal atom/ion ? Give reason in support of your answer.
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometry of coordination compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields.
rows.solution:
The energies of the \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\) orbitals are raised.

In an octahedral field the six ligands approach the metal directly along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes, and these two orbitals are precisely the ones whose lobes point along those axes. An electron in either of them meets an incoming ligand lone pair head on, so the electrostatic repulsion is greatest and the orbital energy rises. The \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\) and \(d_{zx}\) orbitals have their lobes directed between the axes, further from the ligands, so they are repelled less and their energy falls. The five degenerate d orbitals therefore split into a lower set of three, \(t_{2g}\), and an upper set of two, \(e_g\).

rows.stem:
Using crystal field theory, write the electronic configuration of central metal atom/ion of the following :
(i) \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\)
[At. No. : Co = 27]
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometry of coordination compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields.
rows.solution:
In both complexes cobalt is in the \(+3\) oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) has the configuration \(3d^6\). What differs is the strength of the ligand field.

(i) In \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) the fluoride ion is a weak field ligand, so the crystal field splitting energy is smaller than the energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital. The electrons therefore occupy the upper set rather than pair up, giving \(t_{2g}^4 e_g^2\).

(ii) In \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) ammonia is a strong field ligand, so the splitting exceeds the pairing energy and all six electrons crowd into the lower set, giving \(t_{2g}^6 e_g^0\).

rows.stem:
\(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) is paramagnetic while \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) is diamagnetic though both are tetrahedral. Why ?
[Atomic No. : Ni = 28]
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometry of coordination compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields.
rows.solution:
Both complexes are tetrahedral, so the difference lies in the ligands, not the geometry.

In \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) nickel is in the \(+2\) state, so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\), which has two unpaired electrons. The chloride ion is a weak field ligand and cannot supply enough splitting to force those two electrons to pair, so they remain unpaired and the complex is paramagnetic.

In \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) nickel is in the zero oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide is a strong field ligand, and it drives the \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set so that every electron is paired, giving \(3d^{10}\). With no unpaired electron left, the complex is diamagnetic.

rows.stem:
Write hybridization and magnetic behaviour of the complex \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{3-}}\).
[Atomic No. : Fe = 26]
rows.context: The Valence Bond Theory (VBT) explains the formation, magnetic behaviour and geometry of coordination compounds. The Crystal Field Theory (CFT) of coordination compounds is based on the effect of different crystal fields (provided by the ligands taken as point charges), on the degeneracy of d-orbital energies of the central metal atom/ion. The splitting of the d-orbitals provides different electronic arrangements in strong and weak crystal fields.
rows.solution:
Iron is in the \(+3\) oxidation state here, so \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) has the configuration \(3d^5\). The cyanide ion is a strong field ligand, so the five d electrons pair up as far as they can within the lower set, leaving one electron unpaired and vacating two \(3d\) orbitals. Those two vacant \(3d\) orbitals, together with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals, give the hybridisation:

Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\), that is an inner orbital octahedral complex.
Magnetic behaviour: paramagnetic, on account of the single unpaired electron.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) An organic compound (X) has the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\). Draw structures for (X) if it :
(I) does not give Tollen’s test but gives a positive iodoform test.
(II) does not give Tollen’s test and iodoform test but undergoes Aldol condensation.
(III) undergoes Cannizzaro’s reaction.
(ii) Show how each of the following compounds can be converted to benzoic acid :
(I) Acetophenone
(II) Ethyl benzene
rows.solution:
(i) The molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O}\) has one degree of unsaturation, and in each case here that is a carbonyl group.

(I) Failing Tollen's test rules out an aldehyde, so the compound is a ketone; a positive iodoform test requires a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group attached to the rest of the molecule. Both conditions are met by pentan-2-one:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\)

(II) A ketone again, since Tollen's test is negative, but this time without the \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group, and it must still possess an \(\alpha\) hydrogen for aldol condensation. That describes pentan-3-one:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-CH_2-CH_3}\)

(III) Cannizzaro's reaction is given only by an aldehyde that has no \(\alpha\) hydrogen at all, so the carbon next to the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) must be fully substituted. That gives 2,2-dimethylpropanal:
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-CHO}\)

(ii)(I) Acetophenone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO-}\) group on the ring, so sodium hypoiodite cleaves the methyl group away as iodoform and acidification leaves benzoic acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{NaOI}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)
Hot alkaline potassium permanganate followed by acidification achieves the same conversion.

(II) In ethylbenzene the whole two-carbon side chain is oxidised away to a single carboxyl carbon by hot alkaline potassium permanganate, and acidification then liberates the free acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) } \mathrm{H^+}]{\text{(i) } \mathrm{KMnO_4}\text{-}\mathrm{KOH},\ \Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Draw structure of the 2, 4-dinitrophenyl hyzdrazone derivative of benzaldehyde.
(ii) Arrange the following in increasing order of their reactivity towards HCN :
Di-tert. butyl ketone, Acetaldehyde, Acetone
(iii) Give a simple chemical test to distinguish between benzoic acid and ethyl benzoate.
(iv) Write the name of the reagent to convert Ethanenitrile to Ethanal.
(v) Draw the structure of ‘X’ in the following reaction :
cyclohexanol \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CrO_3}}\) ‘X’
rows.solution:
(i) Benzaldehyde condenses with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine at the carbonyl carbon, losing a molecule of water, to give the hydrazone
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH=N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)
in which the two nitro groups sit at positions 2 and 4 of the second ring.

(ii) Addition of \(\mathrm{HCN}\) becomes harder as the carbonyl carbon is made less electrophilic and more crowded, and alkyl groups do both: they push electron density towards the carbonyl carbon and they get in the way of the attacking nucleophile. Two bulky tert-butyl groups hinder the carbonyl most, acetone has two small methyl groups, and acetaldehyde has only one. The increasing order of reactivity is therefore
di-tert-butyl ketone \(<\) acetone \(<\) acetaldehyde.

(iii) Add sodium hydrogen carbonate solution to each. Benzoic acid is a strong enough acid to liberate carbon dioxide from it and gives a brisk effervescence; ethyl benzoate is an ester, is not acidic, and gives no reaction.

(iv) Di-isobutylaluminium hydride, \(\mathrm{DIBAL-H}\), followed by hydrolysis, reduces ethanenitrile to ethanal. Stannous chloride with hydrochloric acid followed by hydrolysis, the Stephen reduction, does the same job.

(v) Chromium trioxide oxidises the secondary alcohol group of cyclohexanol to a carbonyl, so 'X' is cyclohexanone: the same six-membered ring with a \(\mathrm{C=O}\) group in place of the \(\mathrm{CH-OH}\).

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) From the given data of \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}}\) values, answer the following questions :

| \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) | V | Cr | Mn | Fe | Co | Ni | Cu |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | \(-1.18\) | \(-0.91\) | \(-1.18\) | \(-0.44\) | \(-0.28\) | \(-0.25\) | \(+0.34\) |

(I) Why \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) show irregular trend in the above values ?
(II) Why is \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}}\) value exceptionally positive ?
(III) Why \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) value is highly negative ?
(ii) Write the ionic equations for the oxidising action of potassium permanganate for its reaction with \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) in both acidic and alkaline solutions.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) The \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}}\) values vary irregularly because each of them is the net outcome of three separate energy changes, and those changes themselves vary irregularly across the series: the enthalpy of atomisation of the metal, the sum of the first and second ionisation enthalpies \((\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2)\), and the hydration enthalpy of the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion. An irregularity in any one of the three shows up in the electrode potential, and they do not cancel.

(II) Copper is the only metal in the list with a positive value, which means the change from \(\mathrm{Cu}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) in water is not spontaneous. Copper has a high enthalpy of atomisation and high ionisation enthalpies, and the hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), although large, is not large enough to pay for them. The overall energy balance is unfavourable, so \(E^{\circ}\) comes out positive.

(III) The value for manganese is highly negative because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is exceptionally stable: removing two electrons from the manganese atom leaves the half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration, which has extra stability. The metal therefore gives up those two electrons readily, and the oxidation is strongly favoured.

(ii) In acidic solution permanganate is reduced all the way to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), and iodide is oxidised to iodine:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 10\mathrm{I^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 8\mathrm{H_2O} + 5\mathrm{I_2}\)

In alkaline solution the reduction stops at manganese dioxide, and iodide is oxidised further, to iodate:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{I^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{IO_3^-} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Name a member of the lanthanoid series
(I) which exhibits +4 oxidation state
(II) which exhibits +2 oxidation state.
(ii) Why transition metals act as good catalyst ?
(iii) Why Cr has higher melting point than Mn ?
(iv) What happens when acidic solution of potassium permanganate is allowed to stand for sometime ? Give the equation involved. What is this type of reaction called ?
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Cerium exhibits the \(+4\) oxidation state. \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) is favoured because losing the fourth electron leaves the empty \(4f^0\) configuration, which is the stable arrangement of the noble gas xenon.

(II) Europium exhibits the \(+2\) state: \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\) is \(4f^7\), a half-filled f subshell. Ytterbium does the same, \(\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}\) being the completely filled \(4f^{14}\).

(ii) Transition metals make good catalysts for two reasons. They move easily between several oxidation states, so they can accept electrons from one reactant and pass them to another, providing a low energy path. And their partly filled d orbitals let reactant molecules adsorb onto the metal surface and form intermediates there, which brings the reactants together in the right orientation. A finely divided metal also offers a large surface area.

(iii) The melting point of a transition metal is set by the strength of its metallic bonding, which in turn depends on how many unpaired electrons each atom can contribute to that bonding. Chromium is \(3d^5 4s^1\), so it has six unpaired electrons available. Manganese is \(3d^5 4s^2\), and its \(4s\) electrons are already paired, so fewer electrons take part in interatomic bonding. Chromium's metallic bonding is therefore the stronger and its melting point the higher.

(iv) An acidified solution of potassium permanganate is not stable on standing. It slowly oxidises the water it is dissolved in, liberating oxygen, while the permanganate itself is reduced to manganese dioxide, which appears as a brown deposit.
\(4\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{MnO_2} + 3\mathrm{O_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Manganese is reduced from \(+7\) to \(+4\) while oxygen is oxidised from \(-2\) to zero, so oxidation and reduction happen together: this is a redox reaction.

rows.stem:
Calculate emf and \(\Delta\mathrm{G}\) for the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,/\,Mg^{2+}(0.01\ M)\,//\,Ag^{+}(0.001\ M)\,/\,Ag(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = -2.37\) V \(\quad \mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}} = +0.80\) V
[1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), log 10 = 1]
rows.solution:
Magnesium is the anode and silver the cathode in the cell as written, so
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = 0.80 - (-2.37) = 3.17\ \mathrm{V}\)

The cell reaction is
\(\mathrm{Mg(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\)
so two electrons are transferred and \(n = 2\).

By the Nernst equation,
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}\)
\(= 3.17 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{0.01}{(0.001)^2}\)
\(= 3.17 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log 10^{4}\)
\(= 3.17 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\times 4 = 3.17 - 0.118 = 3.052\ \mathrm{V}\)

The free energy change follows from the emf:
\(\Delta G = -nFE_{cell} = -2 \times 96500 \times 3.052 = -589036\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
that is \(-589.036\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). The negative sign confirms that the cell reaction is spontaneous as written.

rows.stem:
For the reaction :
\(\mathrm{2AgCl(s) + H_2(g)\ (0.4\ atm) \longrightarrow 2Ag(s) + 2H^{+}(0.1\ M) + 2Cl^{-}(0.2\ M)}\)
Calculate emf of the cell at 25 °C.
Given : \(\Delta\mathrm{G^{\circ}} = -43500\) J \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
[log 10 = 1, 1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
The standard cell potential is not given directly, but the standard free energy change is, and the two are linked. Two electrons are transferred in the reaction as written, so \(n = 2\):
\(\Delta G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{cell}\)
\(-43500 = -2 \times 96500 \times E^{\circ}_{cell}\)
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = \dfrac{43500}{193000} = 0.225\ \mathrm{V}\)

Silver and silver chloride are both solids, so neither appears in the reaction quotient; the hydrogen is a gas and enters as its partial pressure. The Nernst equation gives
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{H^+}]^2[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2}{p_{\mathrm{H_2}}}\)
\(= 0.225 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{(0.1)^2(0.2)^2}{0.4}\)
\(= 0.225 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log 10^{-3}\)
\(= 0.225 + \dfrac{0.059}{2}\times 3\)
\(= 0.225 + 0.0885 = 0.3135\ \mathrm{V}\)
